re-corallus-caninus.title: Emerald Tree Boa
re-corallus-caninus.summary: A bright green, white-marked tree boa from the rainforests of the Guiana Shield in northern South America. It spends almost its whole life coiled on branches and needs a tall, humid enclosure with sturdy horizontal perches. Best as a display snake with limited, careful handling.
rows: Adults usually 5–6 ft (1.5–1.8 m); females are longer and heavier and can pass 6.5 ft
6 × 2 × 4 ft (L × W × H) minimum for an adult, with several sturdy horizontal perches (removable is best); taller is better
Basking area 85–90°F, general 75–82°F, cool zone and night 72–75°F
75–90%, kept steady; swings cause shedding, breathing and dehydration problems
Nocturnal, but low-intensity UVB is recommended (UVI 2.0–3.0 at the basking area); 12 hours light
Carnivore: frozen-thawed rodents (about 10% of the snake’s weight). Juveniles every 7–10 days, subadults every 10–20 days, adults every 2–4 weeks
Best kept as a minimally handled display snake. Never pull it off a perch; coax it off and lift from below. Juveniles' tails are delicate
Guiana Shield of northern South America (Brazil, the Guianas, Venezuela); rainforest
notes: Babies are orange to brick-red and turn green at about 9–12 months.
The Amazon-basin form is now treated as a separate species, C. batesii.
Trade is regulated under CITES Appendix II.

sources.name: ReptiFiles – Northern Emerald Tree Boa Care Sheet

re-corallus-hortulana.title: Amazon Tree Boa
re-corallus-hortulana.summary: A slender, nocturnal tree boa from northern South America that comes in a huge range of colors, from drab 'garden phase' browns to red, orange and yellow. It's an active display snake that is often defensive, so it is not usually recommended as a first snake.
rows: Usually 4–5 ft (1.2–1.5 m); some reach 6 ft or more
About 4 × 2 × 4 ft (L × W × H) or larger for most adults, with a lattice of horizontal and diagonal branches at different heights and dense cover
60–80% with good airflow; mist so droplets form, then let perches dry
Often more active and more defensive than emerald tree boas, with long teeth. Move it with a hook rather than grabbing it off a perch; best as a display snake
Nocturnal and mostly arboreal, though it sometimes feeds and breeds on the ground
The Guianas, Amazonia and southeastern Brazil
notes: Color varies widely; none of the color phases change care.

sources.name: Dr. Bob's Pet Health Information – Boa and related snake care guide
Big Apple Herp – Amazon tree boa care guide

re-candoia-aspera.title: Viper Boa (New Guinea Ground Boa)
re-candoia-aspera.summary: A short, stocky, harmless boa from New Guinea whose triangular head makes it look like a death adder. It lives on the ground, often burrows, and loves to soak, so it needs a big water bowl and a humid setup.
rows: Ground-dwelling: floor space matters more than height. Adults can live in roughly 20–50 gal-size enclosures with a secure top and thick substrate to burrow in
Daytime around 85°F with a 90°F hot spot; nights should not drop below the mid-70s °F
50–80%. Mist 2–3× a week and give a water bowl big enough to soak in
Rodents; adults about once every 3 weeks (slow metabolism, so watch for obesity). Offer food after dark
More defensive than other Candoia and can be downright nippy; handle calmly and not too often
Nocturnal; terrestrial and semi-burrowing, often sits in its water bowl
New Guinea (Papua, Indonesia and Papua New Guinea) and nearby islands
notes: Lifespan in the wild is not documented.
Can go off feed for long periods without losing much weight.

sources.name: Carille, Natural History and Husbandry of Candoia (IRCF Reptiles & Amphibians 19(2), 2012)

re-eryx-muelleri.title: Saharan Sand Boa (Müller's Sand Boa)
re-eryx-muelleri.summary: A small, docile, burrowing boa from the savannas and desert edges of West and Central Africa. It spends most of its time buried in sand and ambushes prey from below, so deep, loose substrate matters more than a tall enclosure.
rows: Typically 40–60 cm (16–24 in); females are larger and heavier
One adult: at least 60 × 45 × 30 cm (about 24 × 18 × 12 in), with 10–20 cm (4–8 in) of loose sand/soil to burrow in
Warm side 86–90°F (30–32°C), cool side 75–79°F (24–26°C), night 68–72°F (20–22°C). Belly heat works well; no basking lamp needed
Low to moderate (30–50%), with a shallow water bowl; a slightly damp spot helps with shedding
UVB not required; a normal day/night cycle is enough
Mostly small rodents (also lizards in the wild). Adults every 10–14 days, juveniles every 7–10 days. Easy to overfeed
Docile; keep handling brief and support the whole body
West and Central Africa, Senegal to Sudan (savanna and desert, sea level to 500 m)
